one_liner: Node-clustering drop-in replacement for std::list; faster insertion, erasure, sort, and much faster clear/destruction.
what_it_does: plf::list is a header-only, near-drop-in replacement for std::list that keeps the same doubly-linked, order-preserving, pointer-stable semantics but groups nodes into fixed-size memory blocks (default 2048 elements) instead of allocating one node per insertion. It exposes the full std::list interface plus extras (reserve(), shrink_to_fit(), capacity(), memory(), unordered_find_* helpers) and adds within-list splice overloads, but drops single-element/range splicing between two separate list instances (only whole-list splice across instances is supported).
how_it_is_fast: Each memory block keeps a per-block free list of erased slots; on insertion the algorithm searches outward from the target position for a nearby free slot before falling back to allocating a new block, which keeps blocks dense and cuts allocator calls compared to std::list's one-node-per-element scheme. sort() temporarily gathers node pointers into a contiguous array and quicksorts that array instead of mergesorting the linked list in place, which is faster but not guaranteed stable. clear()/destruction skip per-node destructor calls entirely for trivially-destructible element types, which is why those two benchmarks show multiple-order-of-magnitude speedups that don't generalize to non-trivial types.
when_to_use: Hot paths doing frequent insertion/erasure in the middle of a list-like sequence, where std::list's per-node allocation overhead dominates
Trivially-destructible or small POD element types, where the clear()/destructor speedups are largest
Code that needs std::list's pointer/iterator stability under insertion and erasure but wants better cache locality from clustered nodes
GCC/libstdc++ targets on x86-64 similar to the tested environment (MinGW GCC 9.2, Haswell), where the numbers are verified
Projects that can vendor two headers (plf_list.h, plf_tools.h) and want C++98-through-C++23 portability without a build step
when_not_to_use: Code relying on partial (single-element or range) splicing between two separate list objects — only whole-list splice across instances is supported
Code that needs a stable sort; plf::list's pointer-array quicksort is explicitly not guaranteed stable, unlike std::list::sort()
Heavy multi-threaded use beyond simultaneous reads — docs describe only limited concurrency guarantees, not general thread safety
Anything on libc++ or MSVC STL — only libstdc++ (MinGW GCC 9.2) is benchmarked, so gains on those standard libraries are unverified
Very large heap-memory scenarios, where the project's own docs say erasure is only 'best... until very large amounts of memory are involved' without quantifying the falloff

integration.dependencies: none (bundles plf_tools.h / plf_tools_undef.h from the same repo for compiler-feature detection)
integration.min_toolchain: C++98 minimum; auto-detects and uses C++11/14/17/20 features (allocator_traits, variadics, concepts, ranges) when the compiler supports them
integration.platforms: any (portable standard C++, no platform-specific code); benchmarked on x86-64 Windows/MinGW GCC 9.2
integration.thread_safety: Not documented as generally thread-safe. Docs state only simultaneous reads are reliably safe, and that insertion is unaffected by concurrent iteration except at the exact insertion point.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — full std::list API plus extras, but splice() between two separate list instances only supports whole-list transfer, not single-element/range splice

gotchas: sort() is not guaranteed stable, unlike std::list::sort()
The multiple-order-of-magnitude clear()/destruction speedups apply only to trivially-destructible types; non-trivially-destructible types see 811%/1,248% instead of 1,147,900%/6,350%
shrink_to_fit() invalidates all pointers, iterators, and references — unlike ordinary insertion/erasure on plf::list
Splicing an iterator to its own position is undefined behavior, matching std::list (raised as issue #34, closed by the maintainer as user error/UB, not a bug)
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick plf::list over plf::colony/hive when you need std::list's ordered, doubly-linked semantics and its splice/sort/merge/remove API; plf::colony is unordered and only a substitute when insertion order doesn't matter. The other siblings (eastl::vector, fast_vector, veque) target std::vector, not std::list, so they're not alternatives when you specifically need list-style pointer stability and O(1) mid-sequence insertion/erasure.
verified_claims_summary: On the project's own benchmark page (MinGW GCC 9.2 x64, -O2 -march=native, Intel Xeon E3-1241 Haswell, libstdc++), plf::list beat std::list by about 333% average insertion throughput, 77% faster sort, 70% faster reverse, 91% faster remove/remove_if, 63% faster unique, and roughly 25% faster in ordered 'real-world' modification scenarios; the multi-order-of-magnitude clear()/destruction gains apply only to trivially-destructible types (811%/1,248% for non-trivial types).
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-19; all 29 historical GitHub issues are closed) and Zlib-licensed, so it's low-risk to vendor as two header files.
